issues.issue: The issuing entity is named "GPMF Trust 2007-HE1" here while the cover page and the transaction title identify "Greenpoint Mortgage Funding Trust 2007-HE1". The identity of the contracting trust is therefore established by two different names in the same instrument.

Operative terms such as "Repurchase Price", "Substitute HELOC", "Recordation Event" and "Accepted Master Servicing Practices" are used throughout Articles II and IV but defined only in Appendix A to the Indenture, an instrument not attached. A court would have to decide whether the incorporated Indenture definitions or the usage in Sections 2.02–2.04 governs.

Clause (v) sweeps in "any proceeds of the foregoing and any other property owned by the Trust and all other assets included or to be included in the Issuing Entity" after four specific asset categories, leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain. What passed to the Issuing Entity beyond the enumerated items is a genuine ejusdem generis question.

The recital states that the Depositor acquires the HELOCs from the Sponsor "in consideration for its transfer to the Sponsor of the Certificates and the proceeds from the sale of the Notes", whereas this operative paragraph recites the consideration as "the Issuing Entity's delivery of the proceeds from the sale of the Notes and the Certificates to the Sponsor". The recital and the granting language identify different payors of the purchase price.

The obligation to fund additional Draws is imposed on "the Class S Certificateholder", a non-signatory said to agree "by accepting such Certificate", with no stated funding mechanic, timing or remedy for failure. Who bears the Draw-funding risk, and on what terms, is left open on the face of the paragraph.

Section 2.01(a) provides that none of the Securities Administrator, Master Servicer nor Indenture Trustee "shall be obligated or permitted to fund any such Draws", yet this paragraph has the Securities Administrator agreeing to "direct funds" to reimburse Servicer Draw advances. The two paragraphs pull against each other on the Securities Administrator's role in Draw funding.

The paragraph says only that it "is not intended" that any HELOC be a high-cost loan while adding that "the Depositor so represents and recognizes", so whether this is a binding representation or a mere statement of intent is genuinely uncertain. Clause (v) compounds this by referring to the "then current" S&P LEVELS Glossary "which is now Version 5.7 Revised", leaving the operative version indeterminate.

The enumeration uses "(ii)" twice — for the blank Assignment of Mortgage and for the recorded Mortgage — and clause (iv) then requires endorsement "in accordance with clause (ii) above", so which clause is cross-referenced is uncertain. That is a mechanical numbering error that changes what the Sponsor must deliver.

This delivery list requires the "original Credit Line Agreement" and never mentions a Mortgage Note, yet Section 2.02(a) directs the Custodian to confirm each Mortgage File "contains the related Mortgage Note or lost note affidavit" and makes a missing or defective Mortgage Note a repurchase trigger. The delivery obligation and the certification/repurchase machinery describe different documents.

Section 2.01(d)(v) requires an actual title insurance policy (or guaranty title) to be delivered on or before the Closing Date, while this clause allows the Sponsor to satisfy a failure to deliver by furnishing a mere copy within 180 days. Whether non-delivery is a Material Defect under Section 2.02(a) or is cured by this clause is left unresolved.

The certificate must address deposits into "the related Collection Account", a term that appears nowhere else in the Agreement, which elsewhere uses the Master Servicer Collection Account (Sections 2.02(b), 2.03(b)) and the Protected Account (Section 4.06(a)). Which account the certification covers is not settled by the instrument.

"Material Defect" is defined partly by non-conformity "to the review criteria specified in this Section", criteria the Section never separately states, and the layered 90-day, 360-day and second-anniversary periods leave it unclear whether notice and cure are conditions precedent to any repurchase claim. Both the trigger and the timing of the sole remedy are open to opposing readings.

This Section's sole-remedy sentence runs to "the Indenture Trustee, the Issuer, the Depositor and any Noteholder", while Section 2.02(b) states the same limitation for the Issuing Entity, Noteholders, Certificateholders, Indenture Trustee and Owner Trustee and Section 2.03(b) for only the Issuing Entity, Noteholders and Indenture Trustee, with the Note Insurer omitted throughout. Who is bound by the sole remedy cannot be settled by harmonising the three sentences.

The opening words condition the subsection on a purchase made "in accordance with Subsections 2.02(a) or (b) above", but subsection (b) is this very subsection, so the cross-reference is circular. The intended trigger (probably Sections 2.02(a) and 2.03) has to be supplied by construction.

The sole-remedy sentence here names the Issuing Entity, Noteholders, Certificateholders, Indenture Trustee and Owner Trustee, a list that differs from the parallel sentences in Section 2.02(a) and Section 2.03(b) and again omits the Note Insurer. The three provisions cannot be reconciled on the scope of the remedy limitation.

The bracketed parenthetical reserving to the Sponsor the right to enforce breaches "with respect to the HELOCs of the Servicer under the Servicing Agreement" is garbled and opened with a brace rather than a parenthesis, so which party retains which enforcement rights is unclear. The same sentence purports to assign both "rights and obligations", which sits oddly with the closing sentence of Section 2.08 that no obligations are assigned.

This sole-remedy sentence binds the Issuing Entity, Indenture Trustee, Noteholders and Certificateholders, whereas the corresponding sentence in Section 2.03(b) omits Certificateholders and the Note Insurer. The instrument therefore states the same limitation with materially different beneficiaries.

The repurchase obligation turns on a breach that "materially and adversely affects the value of the interests" and on "discovery or receipt of notice", so whether prompt written notice and the 90-day cure window are conditions precedent to a claim, and by what measure materiality is judged, are both open. These are the words on which a repurchase dispute would turn.

The concluding sole-remedy sentence runs only to "the Issuing Entity, the Noteholders or the Indenture Trustee", omitting the Certificateholders and Note Insurer who are expressly covered by the parallel sentences in Sections 2.02(b) and 2.03(a). Whether the Note Insurer's remedies are limited cannot be resolved by reading the three together.

The Sponsor is directed to deliver Substitute HELOC documents "in accordance with the provisions of the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement and Subsection 2.02(b) of this Agreement", but Subsection 2.02(b) concerns remittance of the Repurchase Price, not document delivery, which is governed by Section 2.01(d). The delivery standard for a substitute loan must therefore be supplied by construction.

This Section bars any substitution more than two years after the Closing Date, yet Section 2.05(a) requires substitutions to be deferred until an Opinion of Counsel is delivered and Section 2.02(a) contemplates cure periods running to 360 days and the second anniversary. The absolute bar and the deferral machinery can produce a repurchase obligation with no available substitute remedy.

The deferral of repurchase or substitution until an Opinion of Counsel is obtained can push a substitution past the absolute two-year cut-off imposed by the last sentence of Section 2.04. Which provision prevails when the opinion arrives late is not addressed.

The Indenture Trustee and Owner Trustee "shall require the Sponsor, at its option, to either" substitute or repurchase — the antecedent of "its" is ambiguous as between the Sponsor and the requiring trustees. Who chooses between substitution and repurchase is therefore unsettled.

This representation asserts "full corporate power" although Section 2.06(i) represents the Depositor to be a Delaware limited liability company, and Section 2.06(iii) likewise refers to "corporate action" and "certificate of formation or by-laws". The entity form described in the same series of representations is internally inconsistent.

Clause (vii) is joined to clause (vi) by "or" but has no subject or operative verb — "with respect to any other matter which in the judgment of the Depositor will be determined adversely" — so what is being represented cannot be read off the words. The broken sentence changes the content of the no-litigation representation.

The title representation is given as to "each Mortgage Note and each Mortgage", while Section 2.01(d)(i) requires delivery of the "original Credit Line Agreement" and the assets conveyed under Section 2.01(a) are HELOCs. Whether the warranty reaches the Credit Line Agreements is left to construction.

This Section has the Issuing Entity assigning to the Indenture Trustee the right to enforce the Sponsor's representations in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement, while Section 2.03(a) records that the Sponsor "has retained the right" to enforce breaches with respect to the HELOCs and that the same interest is pledged under the Indenture. Who may sue the Sponsor, and without whose joinder, is not settled by reading the two together.

The Section imposes affirmative duties to monitor, reconcile and "coordinate corrective adjustments" to the Servicer's records, yet closes by entitling the Master Servicer to "conclusively rely on the HELOC data provided to it by the Servicer" with "no liability for any errors in such HELOC data". The two halves of the same provision give opposite answers on responsibility for bad Servicer data.

This paragraph allows photocopying only "at a charge that covers the Master Servicer, Securities Administrator and Indenture Trustee's actual costs", whereas Section 4.07(a) requires the same access to information and documentation regarding the HELOCs to be "afforded without charge". The two access provisions cannot both be applied to the same request.

Clause (iv) — "enforce any other rights or remedies provided by the Mortgage Note or Security Instrument or otherwise available at law or equity" — is an open-ended catch-all following three specific foreclosure-related items. How far the Indenture Trustee's document-execution duty extends beyond the enumerated proceedings is left uncertain.

This paragraph leaves termination of the Servicer to the Master Servicer's own "judgment" and permits it to "take such other action as it deems appropriate", while Section 4.02(b) provides that the Master Servicer "shall ... terminate the rights and obligations of the Servicer" if the Servicer fails to perform. Whether termination is discretionary or mandatory turns on reconciling the two paragraphs.

The mandatory "shall ... terminate the rights and obligations of the Servicer" on any failure to perform is expressed "subject to the preceding paragraph", which commits the same decision to the Master Servicer's judgment under Section 4.02(a). The obligation to terminate is therefore both compulsory and discretionary on the face of the Section.

Section 4.02(b) requires the Master Servicer to "pay the costs of such enforcement at its own expense", while this paragraph entitles it to reimbursement of termination and transfer costs from the Master Servicer Collection Account as Extraordinary Trust Fund Expenses. Which costs fall on the trust rather than the Master Servicer is left to construction.

"The Master Servicer shall require the Servicer to comply" states an obligation without any standard for what requiring compliance entails or what follows from the Servicer's non-compliance. The reach of this one-sentence duty is indeterminate on its face.

The sentence disclaims assumption of "liability for the representations and warranties of the Servicer it replaces" without saying whether that covers only pre-succession breaches or also the successor's own performance of those undertakings. The temporal reach of the disclaimer is genuinely open.

The self-insurance alternative turns on LaSalle Bank maintaining "with any Rating Agency the equivalent of a long term unsecured debt rating of 'A'", and the bond and policy need only be "in such form and amount generally acceptable for entities serving as master servicers or trustees". Both the trigger for self-insurance and the required amount of coverage lack any ascertainable benchmark.

This Section gives the Master Servicer direct power to "master service the HELOCs", consent to assumptions and effectuate foreclosure, while Section 4.01 casts it only as supervisor of the Servicer and Sections 4.05, 4.06 and 4.08 assign those servicing acts to the Servicer under the Servicing Agreement. Whether the Master Servicer may act directly, or only through enforcement against the Servicer, is unresolved.

The certification concerns amounts deposited in "the Protected Account maintained by the Servicer", whereas Section 2.01(e)(iii) uses "the related Collection Account" and Sections 2.02–2.03 use the Master Servicer Collection Account for the same kind of payoff proceeds. The account into which payoffs must go is described differently in different provisions.

The return obligation ends in a circular exception: the file must be returned "unless the related HELOC shall be liquidated, in which case ... the Mortgage File shall be released by the Indenture Trustee or the Custodian to the Servicer or the Master Servicer" — i.e., released again to the party already holding it. What happens to the file on liquidation cannot be read off the sentence.

The sentence "The Master Servicer shall, and (to the extent provided in the Servicing Agreement or this Agreement) enforce the obligation of the Servicer to, provide access" is missing the verb governing "shall", so whether the Master Servicer itself must give access or need only enforce the Servicer's duty is unclear. The grammatical gap changes the content of the obligation.

Access here is to be "afforded without charge", while the third paragraph of Section 4.01 permits the same parties to be charged the Master Servicer's, Securities Administrator's and Indenture Trustee's actual photocopying costs. The two provisions give different answers on cost.

The sentence runs two clauses together without a conjunction — funds "shall be held by the Master Servicer for and on behalf of the Issuing Entity, the Indenture Trustee, the Noteholders and the Certificateholders shall be and remain the sole and exclusive property of the Issuing Entity" — leaving beneficial ownership of the funds and files uncertain. The missing conjunction bears directly on whose property the collections are in an insolvency.

The carve-out that "no earthquake or other additional insurance is to be required" leaves the reach of "other additional insurance" undefined against the enumerated fire, casualty and flood coverages. Whether a particular coverage is excluded or required by law is left to construction.

The paragraph deposits insurance collections into the Master Servicer Collection Account "pursuant to Sections 5.04 and 5.05" and makes them subject to withdrawal "pursuant to Sections 5.05 and 5.06", but Sections 5.04–5.06 govern the Payment Account, withdrawals from it and the Net WAC Cap Rate Carryover Reserve Account, while the Master Servicer Collection Account is governed by Sections 5.02 and 5.03. The cross-references do not match the account named.
